captions.instagram:
How does a commode work?

No motor, no pump: a bent pipe that stays full of water, and a tank that empties in three seconds. Cut a commode in half in 3D, flush it two ways, and see why a fast bucket works and a slow one never does.

→ A commode has no motor: just water, gravity and cleverly shaped pottery.
→ Behind the bowl the outlet bends into a trap that always stays full of water.
→ The bend behind the bowl stays full of water, and that water blocks the gas from the drain.
→ Leave a toilet unused for weeks and the seal evaporates: one flush brings it back.
→ A wash-down pan dumps its water in seconds and pushes the bowl’s contents over the weir.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/commodeclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a commode work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
No motor, no pump: a bent pipe that stays full of water, and a tank that empties in three seconds. Cut a commode in half in 3D, flush it two ways, and see why a fast bucket works and a slow one never does.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/commodeclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/commodeclear

In this video:
• A bowl, a bend and a tank. A commode is one piece of glazed ceramic with a bowl on top and a bent passage, the trap, cast in behind it.
• The trap is a plug made of water. Water always stands in the bend of the trap, level with its lip, the weir.
• A flush is a push or a pull. A wash-down pan, the usual kind in India and Europe, dumps the water in fast and pushes the contents over the weir.
• Two valves and a float. Pressing the button lifts the flush valve and about six litres leave in three seconds, or three litres on the half flush.
• Indian pan, Western pan, same trap. A squat pan and a seated commode are the same machine underneath.
• Then it needs somewhere safe to go. The outlet joins a soil stack whose top is a vent, open above the roof, so that falling water cannot suck the traps dry.
